Green salamanders (Aneides aeneus) exhibit a life history shaped by their montane rock-crevice habitat. At a constant temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], a temperature typical of their cool, moist microenvironments, the eggs require an incubation period of approximately 82 days [ab = approximately 82 days] before hatching, a relatively protracted developmental duration for a plethodontid salamander. The newly emerged neonates possess a modest wet weight of 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of roughly 3 mm, reflecting the limited yolk reserves available for early development. After hatching, the aquatic larval stage is brief or bypassed entirely in this direct-developing species, so the 0.89 centimeter [Lb = 0.89 centimeter] snout-vent length at birth represents the size of a fully formed terrestrial juvenile upon emergence from the egg capsule. This small size at hatching places them among the more diminutive neonates within their genus, necessitating a prolonged period of juvenile growth before they can reach the critical size thresholds required for subsequent developmental milestones.

Juvenile salamanders undergo a steady growth phase, gradually increasing in size as they forage for small invertebrates within their crevice-based territories. Field measurements indicate that individuals attain puberty, marked by the onset of gonadal maturation, at a snout-vent length of 4.6 centimeters [Lp = 4.6 centimeters]. Reaching this size threshold requires a substantial investment of time, as the time since birth at puberty is approximately 7.5 years [tp = approximately 7.5 years] under the prevailing thermal conditions of 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This delayed maturation is consistent with the slow life-history pace observed in many plethodontid salamanders inhabiting stable, resource-limited environments, where energy is prioritized for storage and growth over rapid development. The delay to puberty also stands in contrast to the smaller-bodied and more rapidly developing congeners of the southeastern United States, highlighting the trade-off between attaining a larger body size and the time cost required to reach reproductive competence.

Females that have reached reproductive maturity continue to grow slowly, ultimately achieving an ultimate body size characterized by an adult maximum snout-vent length of 7.1 centimeters [Li = 7.1 centimeters]. Adult females of Aneides aeneus attain an asymptotic body mass of approximately 7.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 7.2 grams], a value towards the higher end of the mass range typical for the genus, consistent with the species' relatively robust body plan adapted for navigating and competing within narrow rock crevices. This substantial adult body size facilitates the production of larger clutches and likely enhances competitive ability for optimal nesting crevices. The integration of size and mass data underscores the species’ relatively large body plan compared to many other Aneides, which may be an adaptation to the thermal stability and food availability of their Appalachian rock-face habitats, where slow growth and high longevity are selectively advantageous.

Reproductive output in the Green salamander reflects its capacity for iteroparity within a single breeding season. Females typically deposit approximately 21 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 21 eggs per clutch], a relatively large fecundity for a plethodontid of its body size. Under optimal conditions, they may produce two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], enabling a substantial maximum annual reproductive effort. These observations are based on captive populations maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C]; at this stable temperature, the combination of clutch size and clutch frequency results in a high potential for population recruitment, provided that suitable nesting crevices and adequate prey resources are available. This reproductive strategy, characterized by moderate-to-large clutches and multiple breeding events within a year, distinguishes Aneides aeneus from many of its congeners that typically produce only a single annual clutch, suggesting a capacity for rapid numerical response to favorable environmental conditions.

Longevity data for this species reveal an impressive maximum lifespan, with individuals documented to persist for up to 20 years [am = up to 20 years] in the wild when maintained at 12 °C [T = 12 °C]. This exceptionally long lifespan, far exceeding the 6.7-year estimate occasionally cited from captive studies, underscores the species’ status as a slow-living, late-maturing amphibian that invests heavily in somatic persistence. The 20-year maximum is more than double the time required to reach puberty, allowing for many seasons of reproductive activity across an individual’s lifetime. Such longevity is ecologically significant in the salamander’s Appalachian rock-crevice habitat, where sporadic recruitment events and stable environmental conditions favor a life-history strategy centered on adult survival and repeated breeding opportunities rather than rapid turnover. The combination of delayed maturation, high annual fecundity, and extreme lifespan positions Aneides aeneus as an outlier among North American plethodontids, exemplifying a bet-hedging approach to life in a temporally variable yet physically stable microhabitat.
